I would keep it simple and stay with the crop pattern that fits Quzhou best: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. I am 67, so I would not choose vegetables or other crops that need too much hand labor, too much market chasing, or too many complicated field decisions. In Quzhou, wheat and maize are the main local grain crops, most farmland follows that rotation, summer rain matches maize, and irrigation is usually more important for wheat. I would use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed, keep fertilizer moderate instead of chasing the highest demonstration yield, irrigate wheat more than maize, and rely on machinery as much as I can. I would manage wheat steadily through spring, harvest it in June, seed maize right after harvest with no-tillage if possible to save labor and keep moisture, and after maize harvest I would prepare again for the next wheat cycle. My plan below assumes I am working 10 mu of land and I am choosing a practical, lower-risk grain system rather than a labor-heavy cash crop system. Sources I used: China Agricultural University on Quzhou’s 2024 wheat-maize results and input levels, a Quzhou field-system study showing over 80% of land in wheat-maize rotation, and China’s agriculture reporting on Quzhou’s crop structure and mechanization: https://news.cau.edu.cn/zhxwnew/ff0f90c1f75b4d04ab700a67a30086d5.htm, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5290742/, https://www.moa.gov.cn/xw/qg/202107/t20210720_6372348.htm
